name: HeliBoard
note_on_repo_location: The canonical repo MOVED from Helium314/HeliBoard to HeliBorg/HeliBoard (org-owned) during the project's life; older issue/discussion links still resolve under the Helium314 path. Cite HeliBorg/HeliBoard for current source.
primary_sources: app/src/main/java/helium314/keyboard/latin/common/Colors.kt (Colors interface, ColorType enum, DefaultColors / DynamicColors / AllColors)
rendering_approach:
HYBRID, but a much thinner hybrid than FUTO's - and the difference is instructive. The dominant mechanism is PER-KEY DRAWING inherited from AOSP LatinIME/OpenBoard: each key has a StateListDrawable and the theme does not replace it, it RE-TINTS it. The `Colors` interface is literally a tinting service, not a drawable-supplying service:

  interface Colors {
      val themeStyle: String
      val hasKeyBorders: Boolean
      fun haveColorsChanged(context: Context): Boolean = false
      @ColorInt fun get(color: ColorType): Int
      fun setColor(drawable: Drawable, color: ColorType)
      fun setColor(view: ImageView, color: ColorType)
      fun setBackground(view: View, color: ColorType)
  }

Every styling operation is 'take this existing drawable/view and apply the color registered for this ColorType' (i.e. a ColorFilter/tint), so a theme can change every COLOR but cannot supply custom key ART - no per-key bitmaps, no custom 9-patches, no per-key outlines or gaps. Layered on top is an optional WHOLE-IMAGE BACKGROUND: all three implementations (`DefaultColors`, `DynamicColors`, `AllColors`) accept an optional `keyboardBackground: Drawable?` painted behind the (then partly transparent) key layer. In the HOLO style with no background image, a `GradientDrawable` is synthesized instead. Net: colors + optional background photo + three fixed icon/shape styles - deliberately narrower than FUTO, and the narrowness is the design's main forward-compat asset.
selector_and_state_model: Deliberately minimal, and this is the clearest trade-off in the item. There is NO rule language, NO selector syntax, and NO match-rule engine - the entire targeting model is the `ColorType` enum, a fixed closed vocabulary of ~43-44 named slots that the RENDERER decides how to apply. A theme author picks colors for named slots; they cannot write 'the key whose code is X' or 'every 2nd key in row 3'. Roles ARE first-class as enum entries rather than as selectors: KEY_BACKGROUND (normal), FUNCTIONAL_KEY_BACKGROUND / FUNCTIONAL_KEY_TEXT (modifiers), ACTION_KEY_BACKGROUND / ACTION_KEY_ICON / ACTION_KEY_POPUP_KEYS_BACKGROUND (Enter/Go), SPACE_BAR_BACKGROUND / SPACE_BAR_TEXT, SHIFT_KEY_ICON. Pressed state is NOT an author-facing token - the pressed appearance is derived automatically from the base color by the brightness helpers (`brighten()`, `darken()`, `brightenOrDarken()`, `adjustLuminosityAndKeepAlpha()`), so 'pressed' is computed, not themed. Disabled/focus states are likewise not exposed. Shift/caps state reaches the theme only through SHIFT_KEY_ICON. Full ColorType list: ACTION_KEY_ICON, ACTION_KEY_BACKGROUND, ACTION_KEY_POPUP_KEYS_BACKGROUND, AUTOFILL_BACKGROUND_CHIP, CLIPBOARD_PIN, EMOJI_CATEGORY, EMOJI_CATEGORY_SELECTED, EMOJI_KEY_TEXT, EMOJI_SEARCH_TEXT, EMOJI_SEARCH_BACKGROUND, FUNCTIONAL_KEY_TEXT, FUNCTIONAL_KEY_BACKGROUND, GESTURE_TRAIL, GESTURE_PREVIEW, KEY_BACKGROUND, KEY_ICON, KEY_TEXT, KEY_HINT_TEXT, KEY_PREVIEW_BACKGROUND, KEY_PREVIEW_TEXT, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_HINT, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_BACKGROUND, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_WORD_BACKGROUND, POPUP_KEYS_BACKGROUND, POPUP_KEY_TEXT, POPUP_KEY_ICON, NAVIGATION_BAR, SHIFT_KEY_ICON, SPACE_BAR_BACKGROUND, SPACE_BAR_TEXT, ONE_HANDED_MODE_BUTTON, REMOVE_SUGGESTION_ICON, STRIP_BACKGROUND, CLIPBOARD_SUGGESTION_BACKGROUND, CLIPBOARD_SUGGESTION_ICON, SUGGESTED_WORD, SUGGESTION_AUTO_CORRECT, SUGGESTION_TYPED_WORD, SUGGESTION_VALID_WORD, TOOL_BAR_EXPAND_KEY, TOOL_BAR_EXPAND_KEY_BACKGROUND, TOOL_BAR_KEY, TOOL_BAR_KEY_ENABLED_BACKGROUND, MAIN_BACKGROUND.
rendering_pipeline: Classic Android View + Canvas, NOT Compose for the keyboard surface. HeliBoard is an AOSP LatinIME / OpenBoard descendant: `InputMethodService` -> KeyboardView/MainKeyboardView with `onDraw` painting keys onto a Canvas, using Drawables and ColorFilters. This entirely sidesteps the Compose-inside-InputMethodService lifecycle-owner problem (no ViewTreeLifecycleOwner / ViewTreeSavedStateRegistryOwner plumbing needed on the keyboard itself) and keeps per-keystroke cost to a view invalidate. Newer versions moved the SETTINGS UI to Compose (`app/src/main/java/helium314/keyboard/settings/screens/`), so the split mirrors FUTO's: Compose for configuration screens, legacy Views for the typing surface. Background-image application is lazily deferred with a `backgroundSetupDone` flag and then materialized once the view has measured: `keyboardBackground = keyboardBackground!!.toBitmap(view.width, view.height).toDrawable(view.context.resources)` - i.e. the drawable is rasterized to exactly the view's pixel dimensions, which is cheap at draw time but has the geometry consequences noted below. Per-keystroke recomposition cost: none, because there is no recomposition.
compositing_scrim_model: The simplest of the three models, and notably there is NO explicit scrim layer. Stack: (1) `keyboardBackground` drawable/bitmap (or a synthesized GradientDrawable for HOLO style with no image) as the bottom layer; (2) key drawables tinted per ColorType on top; (3) labels/icons. Legibility over a photo is achieved by the AUTHOR/USER choosing key background colors WITH ALPHA - the color picker exposes 'whatever color and transparency (the bottom slider) you like', so transparency is a per-color property rather than a global overlay opacity. There is no `opacity` field, no separate `action_bar_opacity`, no dim/brightness overlay control, and no blur. That means: (a) there is no automatic darkening behind keys when a bright photo is chosen - unlike FUTO's computed `(1 - opacity^2) * 0.32 + 0.5` scrim, HeliBoard puts the whole burden on the person picking colors; and (b) an author wanting a scrim must fake it by setting MAIN_BACKGROUND or STRIP_BACKGROUND to a semi-transparent black. The automatic brightness helpers (brighten/darken/brightenOrDarken/adjustLuminosityAndKeepAlpha) act on the KEY colors, not on the background, so they cannot compensate for a bad photo. This is the single biggest functional gap versus FUTO for 'background image done properly'.
asset_types: Very restricted, by design. The theme FILE carries NO assets at all - it is colors-only (see theme_package_manifest_format), so there is no notion of shipping key art. Rendering assets are all app-internal: XML shape/state-list drawables and vector drawables bundled in the APK, selected by one of THREE fixed icon/shape styles - `Material`, `Holo`, `Rounded` (the `themeStyle` property on the Colors interface). Density bucketing is Android's normal res/drawable-*dpi mechanism for those bundled assets, which works precisely BECAUSE assets never travel with a theme. The one user-supplied asset is the BACKGROUND IMAGE, a plain raster picked from the device (not part of the shareable theme), converted to a Bitmap sized to the keyboard view. A custom FONT FILE can also be supplied by the user as a device-local setting. No 9-patch authoring, no SVG import, no Lottie, no shaders, no animated formats.
theme_package_manifest_format:
There is NO zip and NO multi-file package - a HeliBoard theme is a single JSON blob, and its shape CHANGES WITH THE TIER, which is the format's most notable quirk. Export paths, from ColorsScreen.kt: (a) to a file via `Intent.ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT` with filename pattern `"{themeName}.json"`; (b) to the clipboard via `ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip()` with the label `"HeliBoard theme"`. Both call `getColorString()`. TWO serialization shapes:

  * MAIN / MORE COLORS (tier 0 and 1) -> a `SaveThoseColors` record:
      SaveThoseColors(name: String, moreColors: Int, colors: Map<String, Pair<Int?, Boolean>>)
    where each entry maps a color-setting name to (colorValue, isAuto). The nullable Int plus the Boolean is the important bit: a color can be recorded as 'auto' (derive me) rather than as a literal value, so a shared theme can stay adaptive.

  * ALL COLORS (tier 2) -> a FLAT object keyed by ColorType enum NAME:
      {"KEY_BACKGROUND": -14671840, "FUNCTIONAL_KEY_BACKGROUND": -13158601, ..., "<base36-encoded theme name>": 0}
    Colors are raw signed Android ints (ARGB). The theme NAME is smuggled in as a base36-encoded KEY with value 0 rather than as a proper field - a hack that exists because the all-colors format has no envelope.

Day and night themes are stored as two separate preference values (`PREF_THEME_COLORS` and `PREF_THEME_COLORS_NIGHT`) and can be loaded independently, so a full look is really TWO files. The background image is NOT in the JSON - it is a device-local setting, meaning a shared 'theme' never carries its wallpaper. Community distribution is by pasting JSON into GitHub Discussions or third-party repos (Star-Trowa/heliboard-themes, PickleHik3/droid-tings).
token_count_tiering:
The clearest documented three-tier model in the survey, and HeliBoard is explicit that the tiers exist to manage FORWARD-COMPATIBILITY RISK, not just UI complexity. Controlled by `writeUserMoreColors()` with value 0, 1 or 2:
  * Tier 0 - 'Show main colors': 7 fields. Simple themes, described as future-proof and least likely to need updates.
  * Tier 1 - 'Show more colors': 10 fields. Medium complexity. The 10 color-setting keys in KeyboardTheme.kt are exactly: `accent`, `gesture`, `suggestion_text`, `text`, `hint_text`, `keys`, `functional_keys`, `spacebar`, `spacebar_text`, `background` (tier 0's 7 is a subset of these).
  * Tier 2 - 'Show all colors': 41+ fields - every entry of the ColorType enum, currently ~43-44 and GROWING (emoji-search colors were added to this tier after the fact). The UI shows an explicit warning string (`R.string.all_colors_warning`) before the list.
The tiers are not just a progressive-disclosure UI: tiers 0/1 and tier 2 serialize DIFFERENTLY (see theme_package_manifest_format) and carry different durability. Built-in presets are a separate axis: `light`, `dark`, `darker`, `black`, `dynamic`, `blue_gray`, `brown`, `chocolate`, `cloudy`, `forest`, `indigo`, `ocean`, `pink`, `sand`, `violette` (plus legacy `holo_white`), each combinable with the three styles (Material/Holo/Rounded).
theme_versioning_forward_compat: NO schema version field anywhere - and HeliBoard compensates with documentation rather than mechanism, which is exactly the tradeoff worth learning from. The tier-0/1 envelope carries `moreColors: Int` (which tier was saved) but no format version; the tier-2 all-colors format is a bare map with no envelope at all. Missing keys are tolerated (unspecified ColorTypes fall back to computed/default values), and unknown keys are ignored, so old files keep loading. The real breakage is SEMANTIC, not parse-level: when a new ColorType is added (as happened with emoji-search colors), every existing ALL-COLORS theme is silently missing it and renders that new surface with a default that may clash - the theme is not broken, it is INCOMPLETE, and only the author can fix it. This is precisely why the docs frame main colors as 'future-proof and less likely to need updates' and gate all-colors behind a warning string. The lesson: more tokens is not strictly better - every token you expose is a maintenance liability you hand to third-party theme authors forever. FUTO avoids the same trap differently, by giving every manifest field a default AND versioning the format.
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Three sources, cleanly separated into three implementations of the same `Colors` interface (`DefaultColors`, `DynamicColors`, `AllColors`). (1) PRE-BAKED: the ~15 named built-in themes and any user JSON with literal ARGB ints. (2) SYSTEM DYNAMIC: the `dynamic` theme uses Android 12+ Material You wallpaper-derived system colors, implemented as `DynamicColors`; on pre-Android-12 it degrades to the `light` theme. `haveColorsChanged(context)` on the interface exists so the keyboard can detect a wallpaper/system-palette change and rebuild. (3) DERIVED: the `isAuto` flag per color setting - stored as the Boolean in `Map<String, Pair<Int?, Boolean>>` - means 'compute this from the others', and the computation is luminosity manipulation via `brighten()`, `darken()`, `brightenOrDarken()` and `adjustLuminosityAndKeepAlpha()`. This gives useful behavior: set only `background` and `accent` and the rest track sensibly. Notably HeliBoard does NOT extract colors from the user's chosen BACKGROUND IMAGE - no Palette API, no Material Hct/TonalPalette seeding from a photo. That is a real capability gap versus FUTO, which derives an entire Material 3 scheme from a chosen image.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: No validation, no measurement, and no guarantee - legibility is entirely the theme author's and user's responsibility. There is no WCAG contrast-ratio check, no APCA, and no luminance-delta guard comparable to FUTO's 0.08 minimum in its TOML parser; nothing prevents saving or sharing an unreadable theme. What DOES exist: (a) the auto/manual toggle per color, where 'auto' derives a color via brightenOrDarken() from a related one, which usually lands in a legible place because it moves luminosity in the direction that increases separation; (b) a user-facing KEY BORDERS toggle (`hasKeyBorders` on the Colors interface) which is the main escape hatch when keys disappear into a background image - turning borders on restores key boundaries independently of color choice; (c) per-color ALPHA in the picker, so a user who can't read labels over a photo can raise key opacity manually; (d) three shape styles, of which Holo/Rounded change key affordance visibility; (e) font-size scaling as a separate slider. Missing versus FUTO: any automatic scrim, any high-contrast preset mode, any parse-time rejection. For a product shipping user-authored themes to strangers, HeliBoard's model is the one to NOT copy - it works because HeliBoard's audience is self-selecting hobbyists sharing JSON in a GitHub thread, not a consumer theme store.
background_geometry_adaptation: The weakest area, and worth flagging as an explicit anti-pattern. The image is rasterized to the view's exact measured size: `keyboardBackground!!.toBitmap(view.width, view.height).toDrawable(view.context.resources)`. That is a STRETCH to fit, with no normalized crop rect, no content-mode/aspect-fit option, no gravity and no focal point. Consequences: changing keyboard height (HeliBoard has height, padding and font-size sliders), toggling the number row, enabling the toolbar, or entering split / one-handed mode all change view.width/height and therefore re-stretch the image to a different aspect ratio - the art distorts rather than re-crops. HeliBoard's answer to the biggest case is a BRUTE-FORCE one added in 3.0: allow setting the background image for LANDSCAPE AND PORTRAIT SEPARATELY, i.e. two images instead of one adaptive image. That solves rotation but not height sliders, split mode, one-handed mode or tablets. There are also open issues about the background not covering the whole IME area (e.g. the strip/toolbar region and the area below the keyboard). Compare FUTO's normalized `cropping = [0,0,1,1]` fractional rect, which adapts one image to any geometry - that is the design to copy; HeliBoard's is the design to avoid.
layout_locale_independence: Effectively total, and this is the silver lining of having no selector language. Because every theme rule is 'ColorType X = color Y' and the RENDERER decides which surfaces are which ColorType, a HeliBoard theme is completely indifferent to key count, layout and locale. Turning the number row on/off, switching to AZERTY/QWERTZ/Dvorak/non-Latin/custom layouts (HeliBoard supports fully user-defined layouts via its layouts.md format), enabling split keyboard, one-handed mode, the number pad, or an RTL language cannot break a theme - there is nothing positional to break. Toolbar and clipboard-history surfaces are likewise covered by name, not position. The cost of that robustness is exactly the expressiveness gap: you also cannot make ONE key look special, which is what a decorated/illustrated theme needs. HeliBoard sits at one end of the spectrum (maximally layout-robust, minimally expressive) and FUTO's match rules at the other, with FUTO's aspect-ratio-bucket qualifier being the interesting middle: shape-based targeting that is still layout-independent.
non_key_surface_coverage: Excellent coverage - arguably the most COMPLETE surface enumeration of the three, precisely because the model is a flat named-slot list and every surface had to be named. Covered by dedicated ColorType entries: suggestion/prediction strip (STRIP_BACKGROUND, SUGGESTED_WORD, SUGGESTION_AUTO_CORRECT, SUGGESTION_TYPED_WORD, SUGGESTION_VALID_WORD, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_HINT, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_BACKGROUND, MORE_SUGGESTIONS_WORD_BACKGROUND, REMOVE_SUGGESTION_ICON); toolbar (TOOL_BAR_KEY, TOOL_BAR_KEY_ENABLED_BACKGROUND, TOOL_BAR_EXPAND_KEY, TOOL_BAR_EXPAND_KEY_BACKGROUND); emoji panel INCLUDING emoji search (EMOJI_CATEGORY, EMOJI_CATEGORY_SELECTED, EMOJI_KEY_TEXT, EMOJI_SEARCH_TEXT, EMOJI_SEARCH_BACKGROUND); key-preview popup (KEY_PREVIEW_BACKGROUND, KEY_PREVIEW_TEXT); long-press mini-keyboard (POPUP_KEYS_BACKGROUND, POPUP_KEY_TEXT, POPUP_KEY_ICON, ACTION_KEY_POPUP_KEYS_BACKGROUND); clipboard history (CLIPBOARD_PIN, CLIPBOARD_SUGGESTION_BACKGROUND, CLIPBOARD_SUGGESTION_ICON); autofill chips (AUTOFILL_BACKGROUND_CHIP); gesture visuals (GESTURE_TRAIL, GESTURE_PREVIEW); one-handed-mode control (ONE_HANDED_MODE_BUTTON); overall backdrop (MAIN_BACKGROUND); and - notably, and unlike FUTO - the SYSTEM NAVIGATION BAR as a first-class token (NAVIGATION_BAR), with the wiki confirming nav-bar appearance follows the keyboard theme. Not covered: the settings screens themselves are styled by the app's own Material theme, not by ColorType.
sound_haptic_theming: Not themed - identical posture to FUTO. Key sound and vibration are GLOBAL user preferences, not theme properties, and nothing in the exported theme JSON references audio or haptics. What the user gets (from the Preferences wiki page): 'Sound on keypress' on/off plus a keypress SOUND VOLUME slider, and 'Vibrate on keypress' on/off plus a keypress VIBRATION DURATION setting, with a configurable vibration AMPLITUDE proposed for API 26+. Implementation uses stock Android APIs - AudioManager keypress sound effects and Vibrator / HapticFeedbackConstants - with no custom sample loading and no swappable sound packs. So neither open-source Android reference in this survey treats sound as part of a theme; a product wanting sound packs is inventing that dimension, not porting it.
platform_apis_frameworks: Android only, minSdk deliberately low, and notably NO internet permission at all (the app is 100% offline, which is a core selling point and constrains theme delivery - see delivery_installation_pipeline). Stack: InputMethodService + AOSP LatinIME KeyboardView/MainKeyboardView Canvas drawing; Android Drawable / StateListDrawable / GradientDrawable / ColorFilter and ImageView/View tinting via the Colors interface; androidx `toBitmap()` / `toDrawable()` for background rasterization; Android 12+ Material You dynamic system colors for the `dynamic` theme (with a light-theme fallback below 12); `ResourceUtils.isNight(context.resources)` plus SharedPreferences (`PREF_THEME_COLORS`, `PREF_THEME_COLORS_NIGHT`) for day/night; system day/night following on Android 10+ (and some Android 9 builds); Storage Access Framework (`Intent.ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT`) and ClipboardManager for theme export; Jetpack Compose for the newer settings screens only. Kotlin + Java mix. GPL-3.0 licensed - which is a genuine constraint for commercial reuse: you can read and learn from it freely, but copying code into a closed-source keyboard is not permitted.
delivery_installation_pipeline: There is no delivery PIPELINE at all - and that is a deliberate consequence of shipping with no internet permission. Themes reach the keyboard three ways: (1) BUNDLED - the ~15 named presets compiled into the APK; (2) SYSTEM - the `dynamic` theme read live from Android 12+ Material You, no file; (3) MANUAL SIDELOAD - the user is handed a JSON blob (from a GitHub Discussion, a community repo like Star-Trowa/heliboard-themes or PickleHik3/droid-tings, or a friend) and either pastes it from the clipboard or opens a `.json` file through the Storage Access Framework, via the menu at top-right of the 'adjust colors' screen. Where things land on disk: nowhere as a package - the loaded colors are written straight into SharedPreferences as `PREF_THEME_COLORS` / `PREF_THEME_COLORS_NIGHT` strings. There is no themes/ directory, no per-theme asset storage, no signing, no manifest, no version negotiation and no in-app browse/download. The background IMAGE is stored separately as a device-local file/setting and is NOT part of any shareable artifact - so a 'theme' someone shares is colors only and will look different on the recipient's device if they had a background image set. HeliBoard's whole-app settings backup/restore (a JSON of all settings, including learned words) is the only mechanism that moves a complete look between devices.
permission_store_policy_surface: Minimal surface, and intentionally so. Android, so no iOS Full Access analogue. No INTERNET permission is requested - the F-Droid listing and README make 'does not use internet permission and is 100% offline' a headline claim, which structurally eliminates downloadable-theme policy risk but also forecloses any in-app theme store. Theme import is a user-initiated SAF document pick or a clipboard paste, so no storage permission is needed. Distribution is via F-Droid, the IzzyOnDroid repo and GitHub releases rather than Google Play, so Play's User Generated Content policy is not engaged at all - there is no first-party gallery for HeliBoard to moderate. Two constraints a commercial adopter must weigh: (a) GPL-3.0 licensing makes code reuse in a proprietary keyboard non-viable, so this is a DESIGN reference only; (b) glide typing requires a closed-source library the user installs separately, which is a related example of HeliBoard pushing anything with licensing or policy weight outside the app boundary.
memory_performance_budget: No explicit budget is documented, and the platform imposes none comparable to iOS's ~40-60MB extension ceiling - HeliBoard is a normal Android app process. Concrete behaviors that bear on memory: the background image is decoded and then rasterized to a bitmap AT THE VIEW'S EXACT SIZE (`toBitmap(view.width, view.height)`), which caps the retained bitmap at roughly keyboard-area pixels (e.g. ~1080x900 ARGB_8888 is ~3.9MB) rather than at source-image size - a real improvement over holding a full-resolution photo, though the initial decode of the source is still full-size and there is no documented `inSampleSize`/decode-bounds pre-pass. Rasterization is deferred behind a `backgroundSetupDone` flag so it happens once per view configuration, not per draw. No animation exists anywhere in the theme system, so there is no continuous render loop, no GPU context and no frame budget to manage - a meaningful contrast with FUTO's always-on shader path. Color lookups are simple map/enum reads. There is no bitmap cache to leak because there is only ever one background bitmap. Overall the memory posture is accidentally conservative: it is cheap because the feature set is small. [uncertain] - no published profiling numbers or stated ceilings were found in the repo or wiki.
untrusted_theme_validation_security: Small attack surface by construction, but essentially no explicit validation. There is no zip, so ZIP-SLIP and decompression-bomb classes do not apply at all - the only untrusted artifact is a JSON blob of name/int pairs pasted or opened by the user. Parsing an unknown ColorType key is ignored and a missing one falls back to a default, so malformed input degrades rather than crashes. [uncertain] - I did not find explicit try/catch or schema-validation code around theme deserialization in the sources I reached, so a syntactically invalid JSON's behavior (silent reject vs. exception) is unconfirmed. Untrusted IMAGE content is limited to a photo the USER picks from their own device through the system picker, decoded by Android's own decoder - not content shipped by a theme author - which removes the whole 'attacker-supplied image' threat model that FUTO's zip themes carry. There is no code, no shader and no executable content in a HeliBoard theme, so remote-code and GPU-DoS concerns are absent. The realistic worst case is an unreadable or ugly keyboard, not a compromised one. This is a genuinely strong argument for colors-only theme formats when the threat model matters more than the expressiveness.
open_source_reference_availability: Yes - fully open source under GPL-3.0, actively maintained, and the best reference specifically for TOKEN TIERING rather than for background-image rendering. Repo: https://github.com/HeliBorg/HeliBoard (moved from https://github.com/Helium314/HeliBoard; older issue links still resolve there). Key files for theming: `app/src/main/java/helium314/keyboard/latin/common/Colors.kt` (Colors interface, ColorType enum, DefaultColors / DynamicColors / AllColors), `app/src/main/java/helium314/keyboard/keyboard/KeyboardTheme.kt` (theme + style constants, day/night prefs, ColorSetting), `app/src/main/java/helium314/keyboard/settings/screens/ColorsScreen.kt` (tiering, save/load, serialization), plus luminosity helpers (brighten/darken/brightenOrDarken/adjustLuminosityAndKeepAlpha). Docs: wiki page '4. Appearance' is the authoritative user-facing description of the tiers; generated architecture docs at https://deepwiki.com/Helium314/HeliBoard. Lineage matters when reading it: AOSP LatinIME -> OpenBoard -> HeliBoard, so much of the key-drawing code predates the theming work and constrains it. GPL-3.0 means read-and-learn, not copy-into-proprietary.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: In-app only, live, and with no export tooling beyond a JSON dump - simpler than FUTO's two-tier phone/desktop split. The 'adjust colors' screen IS the editor: a color list gated by the three tiers, each row offering an auto/manual toggle and a color picker with a transparency slider, edited live against the running keyboard so the user sees changes immediately (a live preview is inherent because the IME is the thing being restyled). Separate day and night themes are edited independently. The top-right menu handles persistence: save current colors to a file or to the clipboard, and load either a day or a night theme back. There is NO external/web editor, NO theme marketplace, NO thumbnail or preview-image concept, and NO store-listing asset requirement - a shared theme is a JSON string and its 'preview' is whatever screenshot the sharer posts by hand in a GitHub Discussion. Related appearance tooling that is NOT part of the theme file: Material/Holo/Rounded style choice, key borders toggle, keyboard height/padding/font scaling, split-keyboard config per orientation, custom spacebar text, default emoji skin tone, and a custom font file.
cross_platform_token_parity: None - HeliBoard is Android-only with no iOS counterpart and no cross-platform ambition. Portability assessment if you were to borrow the model: the ColorType enum is the MOST portable artifact in this entire survey, because it is pure semantics - 'the action key's background', 'the suggestion strip's background', 'the long-press popup's text' are concepts that exist identically on iOS, so the ~43-token vocabulary transfers to SwiftUI almost verbatim, and the 7/10/41 tiering transfers as a product decision independent of platform. Inherently Android-bound: the `Drawable` / `ColorFilter` / `StateListDrawable` tinting mechanism; `GradientDrawable` synthesis for the Holo style; Material You / Android 12+ dynamic colors (no iOS equivalent - iOS has no wallpaper-color API for extensions); NAVIGATION_BAR (no iOS analogue); `ResourceUtils.isNight()` day/night plumbing (iOS uses `colorScheme` / UITraitCollection instead); density-bucketed bundled drawables; and the SharedPreferences storage model. Verdict: steal the vocabulary and the tiering, not the plumbing.
animation_budget: Not applicable - HeliBoard has NO animated themes and no animated theme format. Background images are static rasters only; there is no Lottie, GIF, video or shader support, no `iTime`-equivalent, and no GPU/EGL context in the theme path. Consequently there is no frame-rate cap to document, no pause-when-idle logic needed, and no animation-related battery cost. The only moving visuals are functional rather than decorative and are not theme-authored: the gesture trail (themed only in COLOR, via GESTURE_TRAIL and GESTURE_PREVIEW) and the key-preview popup pop animation inherited from AOSP LatinIME. This is a clean, defensible position rather than a gap: it is the direct reason HeliBoard's memory and battery posture is trouble-free, and it is the opposite bet from FUTO's always-on shader backgrounds. [uncertain] - no explicit statement was found that animated themes were CONSIDERED AND REJECTED versus simply never proposed.
key_takeaways_for_mochi: The headline lesson is the tiering itself: 7 / 10 / 41+ with an in-app warning on the top tier, and an explicit documented rationale that fewer tokens = more future-proof. Every token you expose is a permanent maintenance liability handed to third-party theme authors.

Adding a token later does not break old themes at parse time - it breaks them SEMANTICALLY, by leaving a new surface unstyled. That is the real forward-compat cost, and it is why the top tier needs a warning.
A colors-only theme format has a near-zero security surface (no zip, no images from strangers, no code) - genuinely worth considering if downloadable themes are a threat-model concern.

A named-slot vocabulary with no selector language is maximally robust to layout/locale/RTL/split changes, at the cost of never being able to make one key special. FUTO's aspect-ratio buckets are the interesting middle ground.

The ColorType enum (~43 entries) is the best available checklist of non-key surfaces you must remember to theme - suggestion strip, toolbar, emoji search, key preview, long-press popup, clipboard, autofill chips, gesture trail, one-handed button, nav bar.

ANTI-PATTERN to avoid: stretching the background image to the measured view size with no normalized crop. It forces a second image for landscape and still distorts under height sliders, split and one-handed mode. Use FUTO's fractional crop rect instead.
ANTI-PATTERN to avoid: no automatic scrim behind keys. Leaving legibility entirely to per-color alpha chosen by the author works for hobbyists sharing JSON, not for a consumer theme store.
